meta.titre: Resultant and Couple: Reducing a System of Coplanar Forces
meta.sous_theme: Resultant force, total moment, couples and equivalent systems

source.epreuve_titre: GCE A/L Pure Mathematics with Mechanics past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: Two porters in Kumba carry a heavy plank between them, one lifting at each end. Together they cancel its weight, but they also decide whether it stays level or tips. A system of forces can have zero total push and still make a body turn, or it can push the body along a line that is not where you expect. At the GCE Advanced Level, questions ask you to reduce several forces to one resultant force or to a couple, often with unknown constants to find. The calculation is a short, repeatable routine.

items: A force written as $F_x\mathbf{i}+F_y\mathbf{j}$ acting at the point $x\mathbf{i}+y\mathbf{j}$ has moment $xF_y-yF_x$ about the origin, anticlockwise positive.
Vectors are added by adding components, so the resultant of several forces is the vector sum.
The perpendicular distance between two parallel lines is measured at right angles to both.
A rigid body is in equilibrium under coplanar forces when the resultant force and the total moment are both zero.

sections.titre: Resultant force, total moment and couples
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Resultant force and total moment.** For forces $\mathbf{F}_i$ acting at points with position vectors $\mathbf{r}_i$ (all in one plane), the resultant force and the total moment about $O$ are

$$
\mathbf{R}=\sum\mathbf{F}_i,\qquad G=\sum\left(x_iF_{iy}-y_iF_{ix}\right) \tag{1}
$$

The magnitude and direction of $\mathbf{R}$ come from $|\mathbf{R}|=\sqrt{R_x^{2}+R_y^{2}}$ and $\tan\theta=\frac{R_y}{R_x}$.

**Couple.** A couple is a pair of equal and opposite forces whose lines of action are parallel but different. Its resultant force is zero, and its moment has magnitude $Fd$, where $d$ is the perpendicular distance between the two lines. Because $\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{0}$, the moment of a couple is the **same about every point**. For forces $\mathbf{F}$ at $\mathbf{a}$ and $-\mathbf{F}$ at $\mathbf{b}$ it is $(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})\times\mathbf{F}$.

**Reducing a system.** Two systems are equivalent when they have the same resultant force and the same total moment about one point (hence about every point). The possible cases are:

| $\mathbf{R}$ | $G$ | The system is equivalent to |
|---|---|---|
| $\mathbf{0}$ | $0$ | nothing: it is in equilibrium |
| $\mathbf{0}$ | $\ne0$ | a couple of moment $G$ |
| $\ne\mathbf{0}$ | any | a single force $\mathbf{R}$ acting along a line, found from $G$ |

For a single force $\mathbf{R}$ the line of action is the set of points $(x,y)$ for which the moment of $\mathbf{R}$ about $O$ equals $G$:

$$
xR_y-yR_x=G \tag{2}
$$

If a system is equivalent to a couple of magnitude $m$, then $\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{0}$ and $G=+m$ or $G=-m$, and the two senses may each give a solution.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question says the forces are equivalent to a couple (possibly of given magnitude) and some constants are unknown.
variantes.contenu_markdown: First put $\sum F_x=0$ and $\sum F_y=0$; these are linear and fix the unknown force components. Then compute $G$ with the signs. The magnitude of the couple is $|G|$. If the magnitude $m$ is given and a position is unknown, solve both $G=m$ and $G=-m$.

variantes.nom: Equivalent single force and its line of action
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the resultant force is not zero and the question asks where the single equivalent force acts.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Find $\mathbf{R}$ and $G$, then write $xR_y-yR_x=G$. This is the Cartesian equation of the line of action. Its intercepts follow by putting $y=0$ or $x=0$: for example $R_y x=G$ gives the intercept on the $x$-axis as $x=\frac{G}{R_y}$ when $R_y\ne0$. If $G=0$ the line passes through the origin.

variantes.nom: A couple from two forces and a distance
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the two forces of a couple are given as vectors at known points, or the distance between their lines is wanted.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Either add the two moments about $O$, or use $(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})\times\mathbf{F}$. Then $d=\dfrac{|G|}{|\mathbf{F}|}$ gives the distance between the lines of action. Check the sense: anticlockwise is positive.

sections.enonce_markdown: The forces $\mathbf{F}_1=(3\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j})$ N, $\mathbf{F}_2=(-\mathbf{i}+q\mathbf{j})$ N and $\mathbf{F}_3=(p\mathbf{i}-6\mathbf{j})$ N act at the points with position vectors $\mathbf{i}$ m, $2\mathbf{j}$ m and $(3\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})$ m respectively. Given that the system is equivalent to a couple, find $p$, $q$, and the magnitude and sense of the couple.

etapes.action: Use the condition for a couple.
etapes.justification: A couple has zero resultant force, so the $x$-components and the $y$-components must each sum to zero.
Both equations are linear in one unknown.

etapes.action: Find the moment of each force about $O$.

etapes.justification: The total moment of a system with zero resultant is the moment of the couple.
For a couple the total moment must be the same about every point; take the point $(1,1)$ and use positions relative to it.

sections.conclusion_markdown: $p=-2$ and $q=4$. The system is equivalent to a couple of magnitude $12\ \mathrm{N\,m}$ acting clockwise.

items.erreur_markdown: A system with zero resultant force is in equilibrium.
items.pourquoi_faux: Zero resultant force removes only the tendency to move in a straight line. If the total moment is not zero the body still turns, and then the system is a couple.
items.correction_markdown: Check both conditions: $\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{0}$ and $G=0$ for equilibrium; $\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{0}$ and $G\ne0$ gives a couple.

items.erreur_markdown: The moment of a couple depends on which point you take moments about.
items.pourquoi_faux: With zero resultant force the total moment is independent of the point, because the correction $\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{R}$ is zero. This is why only one calculation is needed.
items.correction_markdown: The couple has the same moment about every point; computing it about the origin is enough.

items.erreur_markdown: For the forces $6\mathbf{i}\ \mathrm{N}$ at $(0,3)$ and $-6\mathbf{i}\ \mathrm{N}$ at $(0,-1)$, the couple is $6\times3+6\times1=24$ in the anticlockwise sense.
items.pourquoi_faux: The magnitude $24$ is correct but the sense is not. The upper force points to the right and the lower to the left, which is a clockwise turn, so the moment is $-24$.

items.erreur_markdown: For a system equivalent to a couple of magnitude $12\ \mathrm{N\,m}$, only the equation $G=12$ needs to be solved.
items.pourquoi_faux: A magnitude of $12$ means $|G|=12$, which includes the clockwise case $G=-12$. Missing it loses a valid solution.
items.correction_markdown: Solve $G=12$ and $G=-12$ and keep every solution that is possible.

items.erreur_markdown: To find the equivalent single force, take $\mathbf{R}=\sum\mathbf{F}$ and state that it acts through the origin.
items.pourquoi_faux: The single force has the resultant as its vector, but its line of action is fixed by the total moment. It passes through $O$ only if $G=0$.
items.correction_markdown: Use $xR_y-yR_x=G$ to find the line of action.

items.enonce_markdown: A force $\mathbf{F}_1=6\mathbf{i}$ N acts at the point with position vector $3\mathbf{j}$ m and a force $\mathbf{F}_2=-6\mathbf{i}$ N acts at the point with position vector $-\mathbf{j}$ m. Show that the two forces form a couple, and find its magnitude, its sense and the distance between the lines of action.
items.solution_markdown:
The resultant force is $6\mathbf{i}-6\mathbf{i}=\mathbf{0}$, and the forces are parallel and equal and opposite on different lines (at $y=3$ and $y=-1$), so they form a **couple**.

Moments about $O$: $M_1=0(0)-3(6)=-18$ and $M_2=0(0)-(-1)(-6)=-6$, so $G=-24$: the couple has magnitude **$24\ \mathrm{N\,m}$** and acts **clockwise**.

The distance between the lines is $3-(-1)=4\ \mathrm{m}$, and $Fd=6\times4=24\ \mathrm{N\,m}$, which agrees.

items.enonce_markdown: The forces $\mathbf{F}_1=(4\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})$ N and $\mathbf{F}_2=(\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j})$ N act at the points with position vectors $2\mathbf{i}$ m and $\mathbf{j}$ m. Find (a) the magnitude of their resultant and the angle it makes with the positive $x$-axis, (b) their total moment about the origin, and (c) the Cartesian equation of the line of action of the single force equivalent to the system.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\mathbf{R}=(4+1)\mathbf{i}+(1-3)\mathbf{j}=5\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}$, so $|\mathbf{R}|=\sqrt{25+4}=$ **$\sqrt{29}\approx5.39\ \mathrm{N}$**. The angle is $\tan^{-1}\frac{2}{5}=$ **$21.8^\circ$ below the positive $x$-axis**.

(b) $M_1=2(1)-0(4)=2$ and $M_2=0(-3)-1(1)=-1$, so $G=$ **$1\ \mathrm{N\,m}$** anticlockwise.

(c) The line satisfies $xR_y-yR_x=G$: $-2x-5y=1$, that is **$2x+5y+1=0$**. Check: the point $\left(-\frac{1}{2},0\right)$ lies on the line and $R$ acting there has moment $\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)(-2)=1=G$.

items.enonce_markdown: The forces $\mathbf{F}_1=(a\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j})$ N, $\mathbf{F}_2=(-2\mathbf{i}+b\mathbf{j})$ N and $\mathbf{F}_3=(\mathbf{i}-5\mathbf{j})$ N act at the points with position vectors $(2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})$ m, $4\mathbf{j}$ m and $h\mathbf{i}$ m respectively. The three forces reduce to a pure couple whose moment has magnitude $12\ \mathrm{N\,m}$. Determine $a$ and $b$, then every possible value of $h$, stating the sense of the couple in each case.
items.solution_markdown:
Resultant zero: $x$: $a-2+1=0$ gives **$a=1$**. $y$: $3+b-5=0$ gives **$b=2$**.

Moments about $O$: $M_1=2(3)-1(a)=6-1=5$; $M_2=0(b)-4(-2)=8$; $M_3=h(-5)-0(1)=-5h$. So $G=13-5h$.

The magnitude is $12$, so $G=12$ or $G=-12$.
If $G=12$: $13-5h=12$, so **$h=0.2$**, and the couple is **anticlockwise**.
If $G=-12$: $13-5h=-12$, so **$h=5$**, and the couple is **clockwise**.

Check: $13-5(0.2)=12$ and $13-5(5)=-12$.

items_markdown: The resultant is $\mathbf{R}=\sum\mathbf{F}$ and the total moment about $O$ is $G=\sum\left(xF_y-yF_x\right)$, added with their signs.
A couple has $\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{0}$ and moment $Fd$; its moment is the same about every point.
$\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{0}$ and $G=0$ means equilibrium; $\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{0}$ and $G\ne0$ means a couple of moment $G$.
If $\mathbf{R}\ne\mathbf{0}$, the system is equivalent to the single force $\mathbf{R}$ acting along the line $xR_y-yR_x=G$.
A couple of given magnitude $m$ means $G=\pm m$: solve both cases, find the force constants first.
